c.tagline: Faded colonial grandeur on a river island where Africa met Europe

taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before departing since meters are rarely used; colorful horse-drawn calèches are a fun and common way to get around the historic island

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 15 for SAMU medical emergencies; medical facilities are limited, so travel insurance with evacuation coverage is strongly recommended

avoid.reason: Watch for pickpockets and bag-snatchers in the crowded Guet Ndar fishing quarter and around the Faidherbe Bridge, and expect persistent faux guides and touts.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed historic island packed with fading French colonial buildings, the Governor's Palace, and the Grande Mosquée; this is the heart of Saint-Louis and its main draw for visitors.
The mainland district connected to the island by the Faidherbe Bridge, home to the main market, train station, and everyday commercial life away from the tourist core.
A dense, vibrant fishing village on the narrow Langue de Barbarie sandspit, famous for its colorful wooden pirogues lining the beach at dawn and dusk.
A quieter residential and beachfront area near the river mouth, popular for its lighthouse and calmer stretch of coastline.
A rural area on the outskirts of town near the road to Gandiol, known for eco-lodges and access to nearby national parks and bird sanctuaries.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.pay: Cash only; fares negotiated or fixed by route
transit.map: No official transit map; ask locals or hotel staff
transit.note: Public transit is informal; most visitors walk the compact island or use taxis and calèches for longer trips

air: Blaise Diagne International Airport (DSS) in Dakar, ~4 hours away
bus: Frequent buses and shared sept-place taxis from Dakar (~4 hours)

tip.r: Round up or leave 5-10% at restaurants catering to tourists; not expected at small local eateries

landmarks: Pont Faidherbe
The magnificent 1897 iron swing bridge spanning the Senegal River, a 500-metre engineering icon linking mainland Sor to the historic island city.
Île de Saint-Louis (Historic Island)
The UNESCO-listed colonial core of former French West Africa's capital, a grid of balconied, ochre-washed townhouses steeped in faded elegance.
Guet N'Dar Fishing Quarter
A teeming fishermen's district on the Langue de Barbarie sandspit, where thousands of painted pirogues launch daily into the Atlantic surf.
Cathédrale de Saint-Louis
Consecrated in 1828 and among West Africa's oldest churches, its sober neoclassical facade testifies to the city's role as a colonial and missionary capital.
Place Faidherbe
The island's shaded central square framed by the Governance and colonial barracks, long the ceremonial heart of old Saint-Louis.
Palais du Gouverneur (Governance)
The 18th-century governor's palace on Place Faidherbe, once seat of French West Africa's rulers and still the city's most imposing colonial building.
Grande Mosquée de Saint-Louis
The 19th-century mosque of the northern island quarter, unusual for its clock-faced facade, built under French rule for the city's Muslim community.
Musée de la Photographie (MuPho)
A gem of a museum in a restored colonial house, celebrating Saint-Louis' pioneering role in African photography with historic and contemporary images.
Langue de Barbarie National Park
A slender sandspit reserve south of the city where pelicans, terns and flamingos throng the river mouth, explored by tranquil pirogue trips.
Quai Roume Market
A riverside fish market where Guet N'Dar's pirogues unload their daily catch of grouper and shad straight onto the Senegal River quay.

train.note: The Dakar-Saint-Louis line, West Africa's first railway when it opened in 1885, no longer carries passengers; the track and the handsome colonial station survive but nothing scheduled runs on them. Senegal's only working passenger rail is the TER commuter service between Dakar, Diamniadio and Blaise Diagne airport, which comes nowhere near Saint-Louis, and the old Dakar-Bamako line to Mali has been derelict for years. There is no international train service of any kind. Plan every leg to and from Saint-Louis as a road journey.

intl.to: Nouakchott (Mauritania), via the Rosso border about 100 km northeast
intl.op: shared sept-place taxis and minibuses — tickets at the Saint-Louis gare routière, no online booking

bus.note: Everything leaves from the gare routière in Sor on the mainland side, just across the Pont Faidherbe from the island. Sept-place Peugeot estates and minibuses run to Dakar in about 4-5 hours whenever they fill, while Sénégal Dem Dikk (https://www.demdikk.sn/) operates more comfortable scheduled interurban coaches on the same corridor. Heading north, transport goes to Rosso on the Senegal River, where you cross into Mauritania - a crossing with a long-standing reputation for slow formalities and unofficial fees, so allow half a day and confirm visa arrangements before you set off. Bush taxis have no online ticketing: turn up early, pay cash in CFA francs and expect a supplement for luggage.

intl.to: Rosso, Mauritania (Mauritania) - crosses the Senegal River at Rosso, about 100 km northeast of Saint-Louis
intl.op: state-run bac (car ferry) — tickets at the ramp, no online booking

intl.to: Podor & the upper Senegal River (Senegal) - departs from the quay in Saint-Louis
intl.op: Bou el Mogdad river cruise — booked through the operator's office in Saint-Louis

ferry.note: Saint-Louis sits on an island in the mouth of the Senegal River, but the crossings within town are made by bridge - the 1897 Pont Faidherbe to the mainland and a second bridge to the Langue de Barbarie sandspit - so there is no urban ferry. Small pirogues do carry people over to the Guet Ndar fishing quarter and down towards the Langue de Barbarie national park, but they are hired informally at the riverbank rather than run to a timetable. The nearest genuine ferry is the Rosso bac into Mauritania, a crossing of only a few minutes that can involve hours of waiting and haggling, and which a new road bridge is intended to replace. For river travel proper, the restored colonial vessel Bou el Mogdad runs multi-day cruises upstream to Podor roughly between October and May.

half.name: Djoudj National Bird Sanctuary
half.blurb: A UNESCO-listed wetland an hour north, among the world's great bird refuges, where millions of migrants including vast pelican colonies gather each winter.
